rationale: Exact match to the prior campaign-1 point (10 mm graphite), which Core scored PASS on all four requirements: screen 403 K (<=420), FE hotspot 325 K (<=340, 15 K margin), mass 18 kg/m^2 (<=100), thickness 1 cm (<=4 cm). This is the lightest design in the prior record's PASS set (18 kg/m^2, versus 27 for 10 mm aluminium and 89.6 for 10 mm copper), so it is my safe anchor: I am highly confident it meets every requirement because it is directly validated, not extrapolated.

Graphite's FE hotspot was identical (325 K) at 10, 20, and 30 mm in the prior sweep, showing R2 is flat/insensitive to added thickness in that range, i.e. the plate is already past whatever thickness the spreading effect needs to saturate. Trimming 2 mm from the validated 10 mm point is a small step back toward that saturation threshold, so I believe 325 K (or very close to it) still holds, giving mass 14.4 kg/m^2 - 20% lighter than the prior record with low incremental risk.

Continuing the same reasoning: graphite's hotspot did not move at all between 10-30 mm, so the true saturation thickness is at or below 10 mm. 6 mm is a moderate extrapolation below the validated point but still well above the 2 mm scale at which copper cladding (see the 2/3/5 mm copper-on-aluminium prior points, all identical 323 K) demonstrated that local spreading saturates. Mass 10.8 kg/m^2, thickness 6 mm, screening estimate ~400 K (formula ~399+60*t/k, negligible thickness sensitivity) - comfortably inside every limit.

Halfway between the validated 10 mm point and the 2 mm scale shown sufficient for copper cladding to fully realize its spreading benefit. Mass 9.0 kg/m^2. I believe the FE hotspot stays close to the 325 K plateau given the flatness evidence, leaving ample margin to the 340 K limit; mass/thickness limits are not remotely challenged (9 kg/m^2 vs 100, 5 mm vs 40 mm).

More aggressive thinning, motivated directly by the cladding evidence: 2 mm of copper on top of an already-saturated 10 mm aluminium base captured copper's full incremental spreading benefit, and adding a 3rd and 5th mm of copper added nothing further (323 K flat). That implies a couple of millimetres of high/mid-conductivity material at the heated face is enough to establish the lateral spreading path for this geometry. At 4 mm, graphite mass is only 7.2 kg/m^2. Confidence is moderate rather than high since this has no direct prior data point, but the physical reasoning and the large 15 K margin seen at 10 mm give me reasonable belief it still clears 340 K.

My boldest pure-material bet: 3 mm approaches the ~2 mm scale at which copper cladding was shown to already saturate its spreading benefit. Graphite has lower conductivity than copper (150 vs 400 W/mK) so its own saturation thickness could plausibly be somewhat larger, but even a partial shortfall from the 325 K plateau has 15 K of headroom to spend before hitting the 340 K limit. Mass is 5.4 kg/m^2, roughly a third of the prior record's lightest PASS design. I include this as an aggressive, still-reasoned candidate rather than a safe one.

The lightest candidate in this set: mass 3.6 kg/m^2, thickness 2 mm, directly mirroring the 2 mm depth at which copper cladding in the prior sweep already achieved its full spreading benefit atop a saturated base. This is a genuine extrapolation with the least supporting margin of the set, but I include it because the flat R2 trend from 10-30 mm and the fast saturation shown by the copper-cladding data both point toward spreading resistance being dominated by a small near-surface thickness, not by having 10 mm of material. Screening and mass/thickness limits are not remotely at risk here.

Hybrid insurance candidate pairing a thin, high-conductivity copper face (for local spreading right at the heated face, where the prior sweep shows conductivity matters most) with a thin graphite backing to keep mass low. Total thickness 3 mm, mass 8.96 + 3.6 = 12.56 kg/m^2 - still well under the prior record's lightest PASS design (18 kg/m^2) but with a stronger physical case for adequate near-surface spreading than the pure 3 mm graphite option above, since copper's higher conductivity should reach the spreading plateau at a shallower depth than graphite would need alone.

Same copper-face/graphite-backing logic as the previous candidate but with a slightly thicker graphite backing (3 mm) for extra bulk-conduction margin, total thickness 4 mm, mass 8.96 + 5.4 = 14.36 kg/m^2. Positioned as a moderate-confidence fallback between the pure thin-graphite bets and the higher-confidence copper-clad option below, still well under the prior record's lightest validated mass of 18 kg/m^2.

Highest-confidence hybrid: 2 mm of copper directly replicates the exact cladding depth shown in the prior sweep to fully capture copper's spreading benefit (2, 3, and 5 mm copper claddings on aluminium all gave the same 323 K), backed by 3 mm of graphite for bulk conduction margin. Total thickness 5 mm, mass 17.92 + 5.4 = 23.32 kg/m^2. This is heavier than the pure-graphite anchor (18 kg/m^2) but included as the strongest-evidenced insurance point for the low-thickness regime, and is still far lighter than every other prior PASS design besides plain 10 mm graphite (27-89.6 kg/m^2 for the rest).
